newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fails to agree on lira, calls finance ministers.
newsitem.headline: EU fails to agree on lira, calls finance ministers.

text.p: European Union monetary officials failed on Saturday to bring the Italian lira back into the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism, handing the matter to finance ministers to decide in a crisis meeting on Sunday.
Officials told Reuters Italy had asked the monetary committee to let the lira back into the currency grid at a central rate, or parity, of 1,010 lira to the German mark.
This was too weak for its partners, however. They said they wanted a rate of less than 1,000 lira per mark. The lira closed on Friday at around 999 to the mark.
Italian officials had no comment as they left a nearly nine-hour meeting on Saturday evening.
Finance ministers and central bank governors from the 15-nation bloc were to take up the issue at a special meeting at 1330 GMT on Sunday, an official said.
Rome is hoping a return to the ERM will enhance its chances of qualifying for the single European currency in 1999 for which astable two-year stint within the ERM is one of the qualifying criteria.
The ERM is designed to allow member currencies to trade within bands against each other -- for the most part fluctuating by no more than 15 percent from a central rate.
Eleven of the EU's 15 countries are currently members, with only Italy, Sweden, Britain and Greece outside.
Both Italy and Britain were forced out in 1992 after a severe currency crisis nearly brought the system to its knees.

The Italian government does not want the lira to re-enter the grid at too high a level because of the adverse effect on its exports. It said before Saturday's meeting it would like a rate of between 1,000 and 1,050 lira to the German mark.
Neighbour France, however, wants a far less competitive rate because of the impact on its own industry. A figure of 950 lira to the mark has been floated as France's informal goal.
Finance ministers are expected to find a compromise on Sunday. If they failed to agree to let the lira in, the currency was likely to come under intense market pressure on Monday.

German concerns over the future credibility of a single currency have been voiced repeatedly in recent months, punctuated by fears that politics will be the overriding factor in deciding which countries join economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

European countries which want to include their currencies in the planned Euro from 1999 are rushing to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt in 1997 -- necessary if they are to be at the start.

Most are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
Several governments, including Italy, have used controversial one-off budgetary measures to bring their deficits under control.

But some EU monetary officials say that while Italy's turbulent currency history may be a reason to pause, it has nevertheless made enormous strides in the past few years towards becoming a more stable and prosperous economy.
Such an effort cannot be simply brushed aside, they add.
